correctness.rationale: Each tenth-root power has coefficients in {−1,0,1} in the basis 1,X,X²,X³ after cyclotomic reduction. A k-minor therefore has coefficient magnitudes ≤k!≤120. Evaluation at all four primitive tenth roots modulo 401 tests exact zero: a polynomial of degree ≤3 vanishing at four distinct points is zero in the field, and each integral coefficient is smaller in magnitude than 401. This equivalence for each minor makes the maximum of the four modular ranks the complex rank. A separate exact implementation verified the roots and replayed all 63,504 ordered row/column pairs, reproducing (0,0,0,240,6640,56624) for ranks zero through five, the nine displayed affine profiles on every orbit member, and zero mismatches of the rank-three criterion. Row affines act by column relabeling and nonzero column scalings, so the orbit weighting is legitimate. With parity-coset rows the entire fifth-order Fourier matrix appears with columns repeated according to residues modulo five, so rank is the number of occupied residues, giving the pattern (2,2,1,0,0). Choosing the three occupied classes, the singleton class and its representative gives 60 choices; either parity gives 120, and transposing gives a disjoint 120. The exact enumeration proves the converse. The frozen C++ programs and both saved JSON outputs were inspected, not executed.

value.rationale: Order ten is motivated by the early failure of the Fourier full-spark residue criterion; size five is the central, square sampling problem at that order, not an arbitrary chosen slice. The nine exact profiles distinguish full recovery from one or two undetermined directions and show which row choices concentrate each failure. In particular the rank-three equivalence explains the worst loss by a parity/mod-five configuration, a useful benchmark for sampling or exact Fourier-minor work beyond knowing which rows are full spark.
